The first time I unlocked the door to my apartment after closing, I expected to feel triumphant. Instead I felt the particular vertigo of standing inside a promise. The rooms were smaller than I remembered, the ceilings lower, the windows dirtier. The kitchen cabinets hung crookedly, as if exhausted. The bathroom tiles had a yellowed grin. I had bought a place that needed almost everything, and for a moment, everything looked back.

Renovation begins as a fantasy. You scroll through photographs of bright, airy spaces and imagine your life rearranged. Then the contractor arrives with a crowbar, and fantasy meets dust. The first day of demolition was the loudest day of my life. Walls opened like mouths. Under the old drywall we found layers of wallpaper, each pattern a decade’s abandoned skin. Someone had painted over a doorframe so many times that it had become a rounded, soft-edged thing, almost geological. I stood in the rubble and understood that a home is an archaeology site, and every owner leaves a stratum.

For weeks, I lived in a construction zone. My possessions huddled under plastic sheets like refugees. I ate takeout on a folding chair, the only furniture in a room whose floor had been torn down to concrete. At night, the apartment breathed dust. I found it in my hair, my books, the creases of my phone. It was not just dirt; it was the past being sanded into air. I learned to sleep with the sound of a saw in my dreams, a mechanical heartbeat.

The work was not romantic. There were delays and estimates that swelled like bread. There were decisions that felt absurdly consequential: Which white? Which gray? Which tile would I still love in ten years? I stood in aisles of home improvement stores, holding samples under fluorescent light, trying to predict my future self. A renovation forces you to make visible what you value. Do you want openness or privacy? Light or storage? A place for guests or a place for solitude? Every choice is a small confession.

I chose a pale oak floor because it reminded me of a beach I visited as a child, the boards warm under bare feet. I chose a deep green for the kitchen cabinets, a color that felt like a forest after rain. I chose a simple white tile for the bathroom, because I wanted the room to feel clean and uncomplicated. None of these choices were grand. They were just mine. In the middle of so much dust, that mattered.

The transformation happened slowly, then all at once. One afternoon, the floor was finished, and the apartment seemed to exhale. The new cabinets stood straight, their green doors reflecting the window. The light traveled farther than it used to, as if the rooms had expanded. I walked from corner to corner, touching surfaces. It was the same address, the same square footage, but it was no longer the place I had bought. It had become the place I had made.

For a long time after the work ended, I kept noticing the absence of noise. The hammering had become a kind of company, and its disappearance left a ringing silence. I would wake at night expecting the compressor to start, the radio on the counter, the footsteps of men who had briefly shared my address. Then I would remember that the apartment was mine alone again, and the silence felt less like emptiness than like a room I had finally earned.

Yet the renovation taught me that making is never finished. A home is not a museum piece. Within a week, the first scratch appeared on the floor, a thin silver line from moving a chair. I felt a pang, then relief. The scratch meant the floor was living. The cabinets would warm with use. The grout would gray. The walls would collect the small marks of daily life. A home is not a photograph; it is a body, and bodies bear evidence of time.

I also learned something about control. I had believed a renovation was a project to manage, a list to complete. But the apartment had its own opinions. The plumbing resisted. The windows leaked. The contractor disappeared for three days and returned with a story I did not entirely believe. I could either fight every surprise or accept that some things would remain imperfect. I chose, imperfectly, to accept. The ceiling still has a slight unevenness in the corner. I notice it only when the light is low. It reminds me that I did not conquer the space; I collaborated with it.

Before the renovation, I thought a beautiful home would change my life. Now I know it changed my attention. I notice morning light on the green cabinets. I hear the quiet of a room that is finally at rest. I sit on the floor sometimes, because I can, because it is mine, because the dust is gone. The apartment is not a promise anymore. It is a practice. It is a place where I keep learning how to live with what I have, how to repair what is broken, and how to leave room for the scratches that will come.

The cabinets are going to get scratched, the grout is going to get dirty, the walls are going to get marks. That's just life. So you learn to accept. There's a little unevenness in the ceiling that I can only see at night when the light is low. And I'm okay with it. I just learned that things can be imperfect. And I very much enjoy living in this space. But I think it changed my perception of beauty. Now I just enjoy the light coming in the morning and touching the green cabinets. And I hear silence. Sometimes I just sit on the floor because I can. And it's just nice to just sit there and enjoy that I live in this space. So it's not a dream anymore. It's real. And it's a very nice reality.

Rewrite the draft below so it reads like a person wrote it. Keep every fact and the meaning, keep it at about 573 words, and do not add new claims. Plain prose only.

Draft:
When a familiar product suddenly costs more, the first reaction is often frustration. The receipt looks wrong, the budget tightens, and loyalty begins to feel one-sided. Yet a price increase is not automatically unfair. The real question is not whether prices should ever rise, but whether a particular increase is necessary, transparent, and matched by value. A price increase can be justified when it reflects genuine cost pressures and is communicated honestly; it becomes harmful when it is imposed opportunistically on captive customers.

Costs rarely stay still. Raw materials, energy, transportation, labor, and compliance with regulations can all become more expensive. If a company absorbs every increase indefinitely, it may cut corners, reduce staff, delay maintenance, or eventually fail. None of those outcomes serves customers well. A modest price adjustment can preserve product quality, reliable service, and jobs. In this sense, paying a little more may be preferable to receiving a deteriorating version of the same product. A price increase can therefore be a sign of a functioning business rather than simple greed.

Consumers, however, experience price increases unevenly. For a household with a comfortable income, an extra dollar may be invisible. For someone living paycheck to paycheck, the same increase can force difficult choices. This is why fairness matters. A price rise that arrives without explanation, while quality falls or executive bonuses soar, feels like exploitation rather than necessity. Trust erodes quickly when customers suspect they are being charged more simply because they have few alternatives. Yet consumers are not powerless; they can switch brands, postpone purchases, or choose substitutes, and companies know this.

Businesses therefore need to treat pricing as a form of communication. They should explain the reasons for an increase, give advance notice where possible, and avoid deceptive tricks such as shrinking the package while claiming the price is unchanged. They can also soften the impact through loyalty discounts, bulk options, or lower-cost versions. Such measures do not eliminate the pain, but they show respect for customers and acknowledge that price is not just an economic signal; it is a relationship. Transparency does not guarantee acceptance, but it preserves dignity and gives customers a fair chance to decide.

Competition provides an important check. In a crowded market, a company that raises prices too far or too fast will lose customers to rivals. That discipline tends to keep increases tied to value. In markets with little competition, especially for essentials, the same increase may be harder to resist and may require public scrutiny. Regulators may also need to step in where price hikes reflect abuse of dominance rather than genuine cost recovery. The context matters: a luxury gadget, a subscription service, and a basic medicine do not carry the same moral weight.

Ultimately, a product price increase should be judged by three tests: Is it necessary? Is it honest? Does the customer receive something worth paying for? When the answer is yes, an increase can be reasonable and even responsible. When the answer is no, it is simply a transfer of burden from company to consumer. Companies have the right to protect their margins, but they do not have the right to hide behind vague excuses. Consumers, in turn, should ask questions, compare alternatives, and reward businesses that explain themselves clearly. A price increase is not a betrayal by itself. It becomes one only when it breaks the unspoken bargain that value and trust will rise along with the cost.
items.raw:
We often hear very negative thoughts around price increases for any product. The consumer feels betrayed. The consumer thinks, the same product, same brand, why is it more expensive? The price increase is not always a bad thing, but I think what is bad is when it is not justified, it is not transparent, and the value is not being provided. So a price increase is justified when the supplier or the manufacturer faces a real cost increase. Things are becoming more expensive, raw materials, energy, transport, labor, compliance. If you don't pass it through, you might have to reduce the quality of the product, or reduce the staff, or reduce maintenance, or you might go bankrupt. Which is not very convenient for the customer either. So sometimes, a small price increase is better than the quality of the product falling. And then, the customer says, okay, I'm paying more than before, but I get the same product or the same service that I always got. It's a very human thing, that the consumer is always looking for the minimum price. But if we make the most affordable product, in general, the quality is going to suffer. So we need to find a balance.

But then, of course, the consumer feels very badly when it's a very modest income. So the same price increase is not perceived in the same way. So it's very important to do it in a transparent way. And to explain to the customer why we are doing it. For example, we need to pay more for raw material or we need to pay more for transport or energy. So the customer can understand it. And sometimes the consumer feels very betrayed, when the price goes up, but the quality goes down. And that's very common. That's very difficult. So it's very important that the company does it in a transparent way, and it needs to communicate to the customer. The customer can always change product or brand, of course, that's true. The company knows that. So it's very important that the company does not do the price increase in a very tricky way. Like reducing the size of the product and saying, "I haven't increased the price." That's very tricky. And it's very bad. Or if the company can give loyalty discounts, bulk discounts, or give cheaper options to the customer. That's very good. So the customer can decide to buy the same quantity, but it's more expensive. Or buy a bit less, but the same quality.

And the other thing is that if there are many competitors, the customer can switch. So the company, in a competitive market, cannot increase the price a lot, otherwise it will lose customers. In very non-competitive markets, the customer is very captive. So in that case, the price increase is more difficult for the customer, and maybe some regulation is needed. Or scrutiny from the public, to see whether the price increase is justified. So a price increase is never a betrayal, I think. But it should be very well explained and justified and transparent. And the value has to be given to the customer. That's very important. If the price goes up and the value is given, the customer is happy. So it's very important that the consumer also claims their rights, asks questions and compares prices and demands the value. That's very important.

items.raw: I think we all get annoyed when prices go up for products that we know and buy all the time. We buy some shampoo and it costs 10 pounds more and then we're like, what the hell? And we say it's not fair, loyalty and so on. But I think it's not so simple. It's not that a price should never go up. Prices always go up. It depends on why it goes up, how transparent it is and how much value you get in return. So, I think price increases are justified if they're very transparent, very justifiable and they're not abusive. For example, the raw materials, the logistics, the energy, the labor, the compliance. Everything costs more. So if a company absorbs all the increase, they'll start cutting costs, cutting quality, cutting their people, cutting maintenance and eventually go bankrupt. So it's a natural thing. I think that paying a little bit more and getting the same quality, the same service, the same product, is better than paying the same amount and getting a worse product. So it's actually a good sign of a well-functioning company. But of course, the price increase is not equal for everybody. If you earn a good salary, for you, £1 extra per product doesn't mean anything. But for somebody that lives from paycheck to paycheck, it's very important. So it's very easy to exploit the people and to say that it's fine, that prices are going up while quality is going down, bonuses are going up and so on. So transparency is very important. But at the same time, consumers have choices. They can move to another brand, they can wait, they can buy substitutes. So companies know that. They can do loyalty discounts, they can do bulk purchases, they can do a low-price version. So it's a very important aspect. A price is a relationship, not just a number. And if you're transparent, it doesn't mean they're going to accept the increase, but it's more fair and dignified. Also, competition plays a big role. If a market is very competitive and you increase the price too much, you're going to lose customers. So competition puts a limit and creates a very good benchmark.
